context: civil-dominant · linear progress by chainage, span or kilometre

brief.intro: Linear and civil infrastructure covers roads, bridges, pipelines and port/marine works — projects that stretch along a corridor or across a site rather than rising as a single building. The scope is dominated by earthworks, pavement or trackbed formation, and either structures (bridges, piers, quay walls) or buried/at-grade networks (pipelines, drainage, cabling); mechanical and electrical systems are a lighter overlay, such as lighting, ITS/SCADA, cathodic protection or pump stations. Because the work is linear, progress is usually measured and reported per kilometre, per span or per chainage rather than as one building percent-complete, and the programme is paced by how fast the earthworks or structural fronts can advance and by the quantities they must move or place. Commissioning here means proof-and-acceptance testing — load tests, hydrotests, survey verification — and handover to the operating authority, not a plant start-up. Access, right-of-way, existing-utility diversions and permitting or possession windows are frequently the real schedule constraint, more than the physical construction itself.

scope.name: Enabling works & utility diversions
scope.desc: Access tracks, temporary works, environmental controls, and diverting any existing utilities in the corridor.

scope.name: Earthworks & formation
scope.desc: Cut/fill, subgrade preparation, embankments and ground improvement along the alignment.

scope.name: Structures
scope.desc: Bridges, culverts, pump-station or plant-room civils, and quay/jetty/marine structures on the route.

scope.name: Pavement / trackform / pipeline laying
scope.desc: Asphalt or concrete pavement, buried pipeline trenching and jointing, or trackbed — as applicable to the asset.

scope.name: Drainage & buried services
scope.desc: Culverts, attenuation, cable/pipe crossings, duct banks and chambers.

scope.name: Structural / mechanical elements
scope.desc: Bridge bearings and expansion joints, gates, or pipeline valves and fittings.

scope.name: Electrical power & lighting
scope.desc: Feeders, substations/kiosks, road/area/navigation lighting and earthing.

scope.name: Instrumentation, ITS / SCADA & cathodic protection
scope.desc: Traffic systems, telemetry and corrosion-protection systems specific to the asset type.

scope.name: Testing & proof acceptance
scope.desc: Load testing, hydrotest/pigging, survey verification and functional proving of drainage and pump stations.

scope.name: Handover to operator
scope.desc: As-built documentation, regulatory acceptance and operator training/handover.

glossary.plain: distance measured along the route from a fixed starting point — the standard way progress and location are reported on linear works.
the prepared ground surface a pavement, trackbed or structure is built on, after cut/fill and compaction.
pressure-testing a pipeline with water to prove it holds pressure and has no leaks before it carries product.
running a device ('pig') through a pipeline to clean it, inspect it, or separate batches of product.
an electrical system that prevents buried steel pipelines or marine steel structures from corroding.
Intelligent Transport Systems — traffic signals, variable message signs, tolling and the SCADA/comms tying them together.
a fixed period (e.g. a rail or lane closure) during which a linear asset can be worked on — often the real schedule constraint.
a physical test (loading a bridge, pressurising a pipe) that demonstrates a structure or system performs as designed before acceptance.

must_get_right: Progress is per chainage, kilometre or span, not percent-of-building — track and report it that way, and plan the front(s) of advance against realistic plant/crew output rates.
Existing-utility diversions, permits and possession/closure windows are frequently the true critical path — sequence around them, don't assume the physical works are the constraint.
The final proof/acceptance test (load test, hydrotest, survey) is a hard gate to handover — protect real time for it and expect conditional re-tests.
MEP here is a lighter overlay, not the driver — don't over-schedule it at the expense of the earthworks/structures front(s) that actually pace the job.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. For linear works, activities are typically chainage-banded (per kilometre, per span, per section) rather than purely per-trade, so quantity and productivity rates drive durations. The network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual and possession-window milestones; total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Earthworks and pavement typically run a 6-day, weather-sensitive calendar with a wet-season allowance embedded; structures follow a pour/lift cycle calendar; pipeline welding and jointing follows the crew-spread's calendar; testing and commissioning are scheduled against possession or closure windows rather than a fixed weekly calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path typically runs utility diversion / possession → earthworks and formation advance, paced by cut/fill haul and plant output → structures (bridges, piers, quay) on the critical alignment → pavement, trackform or pipe-lay following a fixed distance behind → final proof/acceptance testing → handover. On multi-span or multi-kilometre works, the critical path usually sits on the slowest-advancing front rather than on any single activity.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Right-of-way and land access are secured; utility diversions are complete ahead of the earthworks front; design is frozen per section; plant spreads mobilise once and work continuously along the alignment without remobilisation.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Long-lead items are fewer than on a plant project, but possession/closure windows are an equally hard constraint. Both are tracked as milestones:

rows: Aligned to the structures & tie-in front

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Right-of-way, existing-utility crossings, and possession or closure windows (rail, road, marine tidal) are frequently the true constraint on when work can proceed. Plant-spread mobilisation over a long corridor, and environmental or seasonal restrictions (wet season, marine tidal windows), further limit the working front.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: variable ground conditions, utility-diversion delays, possession-window slippage, and re-test loops on hydrotest or load test. Schedule contingency is held before final proof/acceptance testing, before handover, and at structure crossings or tie-in points rather than spread thinly along the alignment.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary, by section/chainage) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
